title: Young Learners vs. Adults

pts: Young learners, especially under roughly age seven, are still developing abstract reasoning — explicit grammar explanation often lands poorly.
Concrete, contextualised presentation works where an abstract rule statement would not yet be processed meaningfully.
This is a developmental constraint, not a matter of young learners being 'less capable' language learners.
points.who: Piagetian developmental stages, applied to YL pedagogy by Lynne Cameron

v: A cloth bag with five real objects (a banana, a pencil, a ball, a spoon, a toy car)

items: Hold up the bag and shake it. ‘What’s in the magic bag?’
Let a child put a hand in without looking and feel an object. The class guesses. Model: Is it a ball?
The child takes it out. The class names it together.
Repeat with the other objects. After the third, children ask the question themselves.
Hide one object behind your back. ‘What’s missing?’ Children answer.
For older children (9–11), describe an object without naming it: It’s yellow. You can eat it.
Use objects from learners’ homes for a follow-up lesson.
Support: children point and repeat.
Stretch: children describe the object before taking it out.

lines: For young children: teach Is it a ball? Yes, it is. / No, it isn’t. through the game; do not explain question inversion.
For adults: the same question can be presented as a pattern (Is it…? inverts subject and verb) and practised in a quick information-gap task.

blocks.x: Cameron (2001) notes that young learners use language to do things, not to talk about language.

body: Purpose: to illustrate concrete, hands-on presentation. Content: a colourful cloth bag with a child’s hand reaching in, and five objects spilling out around it. Speech bubbles from children: ‘Is it a ball?’ ‘Is it a banana?’ Style: bright, warm, child-friendly illustration. Board version: not applicable.

items: Read Along by Google (free Android app). A reading assistant that listens to children read aloud and gives feedback; stories are available in English and several Indian languages. Best for independent reading practice after lessons. [VERIFY current language list.]

blocks.x: Real objects: nothing works better with young children.

pts: Young learners need shorter, more varied activities strung together across a lesson.
Adults can sustain longer, more analytical single tasks without the same need for frequent variety.
A lesson plan built for adult attention span, used unchanged with children, will visibly lose the class partway through.

v: Song; picture cards; a short story; drawing paper

items: Song (5 min): an action song with the target words.
Picture cards (7 min): show, say, point.
Game (8 min): ‘Simon says’ or a card-matching game.
Story (10 min): a short picture story using the same words, with children joining in on repeated lines.
Draw and label (10 min): children draw a scene from the story and label two things.
Vary energy: stir (song, game) and settle (story, drawing) in turn.
For adults, the same topic might be one 30-minute task and one 10-minute review.
Shorten each activity for very young children (4–6).
Support: children who cannot yet write draw only and tell the teacher the words.
Stretch: children write a sentence under their drawing.

lines: Stirring (raise energy): songs with actions, running dictation, ‘Simon says’.
Settling (calm the class): colouring, story listening, copying, quiet reading.

blocks.x: A rough rule for young learners: in class, many children will attend well to one activity for somewhere around their age in minutes, plus a little. [Treat this as a planning heuristic, not a research finding.]

body: Purpose: to show variety in a young-learner lesson. Content: a wavy line across a 40-minute timeline, rising (stir) and falling (settle) five times. Icons at each peak and trough: musical note, cards, game, book, crayons. Style: playful, bright. Board version: not applicable.

items: YouTube Kids (free) or teacher-selected song videos. Preview every video before class. [Check school policy on video use.]

blocks.x: Sing songs yourself; children do not mind if your voice is imperfect.

pts: For young learners, games, songs and stories are not supplementary extras — they are the primary vehicle for language input.
Play-based tasks provide repetition and context without triggering the disengagement a drill-based approach would cause at this age.
This reframes 'fun' activities as core methodology for this age group, not a reward for finishing 'real' work.
points.who: Lynne Cameron, "Teaching Languages to Young Learners"

v: A simple repetitive story (see model language); pictures

items: Tell a story with a repeated line. Children listen the first time.
Second time, they join in the repeated line with actions.
Third time, some children take roles and speak the lines.
Children retell the story in small groups using the pictures.
Keep the story for another day and repeat it with new children taking roles.
Use a folk tale from learners’ own region, told in English with key words in the home language.
Turn the story into a short class play for an assembly.
Support: children only do the chorus actions.
Stretch: children add a new animal to the story with their own line.

lines: A little mouse was hungry. She went to the cat. ‘Can I have some food, please?’ ‘No!’ said the cat. She went to the dog. ‘Can I have some food, please?’ ‘No!’ said the dog. She went to the elephant. ‘Can I have some food, please?’ ‘Yes!’ said the elephant, and gave her a big banana.

blocks.x: Why play is methodology: games and stories give repetition without boredom, context without explanation, and a reason to use language (Wright, Betteridge and Buckby 2006).

body: Purpose: picture cards for retelling. Content: five cards in sequence: a small mouse holding its stomach; the mouse and a cat shaking its head; the mouse and a dog shaking its head; the mouse and a friendly elephant; the mouse holding a banana, smiling. Style: simple, bold, child-friendly; large enough to show to a class. Board version: stick animals.

items: StoryWeaver (free). Many picture books for young learners, some with repetitive structures, in English and Indian languages.

blocks.x: Hand-drawn picture cards on chart paper.

body: Repetitive stories are found in the oral traditions of many languages. Children often know such stories already in Kannada, Hindi, Tamil or another home language. Telling a familiar story in English lets them use their knowledge of the plot to understand the new language.

pts: Adult learners can reflect explicitly on their own learning strategies in ways young children generally cannot yet.
This makes strategy training (Unit 19) and explicit grammar noticing (Unit 6) far more directly usable with adults.
Metacognitive tasks aimed at young learners need to be far more concrete and guided.

items: Learners complete a short questionnaire about how they study English (see model language).
In pairs, they compare answers.
Introduce two or three strategies with evidence behind them (self-testing, spaced review, using new words in sentences).
Each learner chooses one new strategy to try for two weeks.
After two weeks, learners report back: did it help?
With younger teenagers, use a simpler checklist with pictures.
Link to the strategy experiment in Unit 2.
Support: questionnaire in the home language.
Stretch: learners research one strategy and present it to the class.

lines: When I learn new words, I… (copy them / test myself / use them in sentences / listen to them).
When I don’t understand something in English, I… (ask / guess / skip / use a dictionary).
I study English… (every day / before tests / only in class).

blocks.x: Metacognition, thinking about one’s own thinking, develops with age. Adults and older teenagers can use it to plan and evaluate their learning in ways young children usually cannot yet.

body: Figure 16.4 A learner looking at their own learning

Purpose: to illustrate metacognition. Content: an adult learner at a desk with a notebook; above them, a thought bubble showing a smaller version of the same learner studying, with a magnifying glass over it. Labels: ‘plan’, ‘monitor’, ‘evaluate’. Style: thoughtful, clean. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Forms (free). The questionnaire with instant class summary.

blocks.x: The questionnaire on paper; results tallied on the board.

pts: Children are often extrinsically motivated by teacher or parent approval more than by any instrumental language goal.
Adults more often bring their own instrumental or integrative motivation, as mapped in Unit 2's needs analysis.
Motivational framing that works for one age group can fall flat, or even backfire, with the other.

items: Young learners: show pictures (a cartoon character, a friend, a game, a teacher smiling). ‘Which one makes you happy to learn English?’
Teenagers: ‘Where do you meet English you like?’ (games, songs, social media, sport).
Adults: ‘What do you need English for in the next year?’
Note answers and connect lesson topics to them.
Revisit the answers each term.
With teenagers, a quick anonymous poll.
With adults, link to the future-self letter (Unit 2).
Support: pictures and home-language answers.
Stretch: learners explain their reason in two sentences.

lines: Young children: pleasing the teacher and parents, enjoying games and songs, friends.
Teenagers: identity, peers, games, music, social media, future plans.
Adults: jobs, exams, children’s schooling, travel, personal goals (Unit 2).

blocks.x: Framing a task: for children, Let’s sing and win stars!; for adults, This will help you in your job interview.

body: Purpose: to contrast motivation by age. Content: three panels: a child with a star sticker and a smiling teacher; a teenager with headphones and a phone showing a game; an adult with a folder labelled ‘interview’. Style: inclusive, friendly. Board version: not applicable.

items: Mentimeter (free basic version) for teenagers and adults.

blocks.x: Pictures and a show of hands for children.

points.sub: Calibrate by age, not by rule
pts: Young learners are often less self-conscious about errors than teenagers or adults, changing how correction (Unit 8) should be calibrated.
Teenagers, in particular, can be highly sensitive to public correction in front of peers.
The correction hierarchy stays the same; the frequency and visibility of correction should adjust to the age group.

items: With young children, correct mainly by modelling: repeat the correct form naturally in your reply.
With teenagers, avoid public correction of individuals when possible; use delayed, anonymous feedback (Unit 8).
With adults, ask how they prefer to be corrected and respect their answer where possible.
Watch reactions and adjust.
Offer adults a choice: ‘Would you like me to correct you during speaking, or after?’
Support: more private, less frequent correction for anxious learners of any age.
Stretch: more explicit correction for confident adults who ask for it.

lines: Child: Me go park! → T: Oh, you went to the park! Lovely!
Teenager: error noted during pair work; addressed later as an anonymous board sentence.
Adult: Would you like me to correct your pronunciation now, or at the end?

body: Purpose: to show calibrated correction. Content: a volume dial with three settings labelled ‘children: gentle modelling’, ‘teenagers: private and delayed’, ‘adults: ask and agree’. Style: simple iconic dial. Board version: not applicable.

items: Padlet (free plan) for anonymous feedback walls with teenagers.

pts: Don't assume L1 literacy in young learners — pre-literate children need oral-first approaches regardless of the target language focus.
Written activities designed for literate adults can accidentally test literacy rather than language ability with young children.
Check literacy status as part of the learner profile (Unit 2), not as an afterthought.

v: Simple reading task in the home language and English

items: Before planning written work, check each learner’s literacy in their home language and in English with a short, friendly task.
For pre-literate or emerging readers, plan oral-first activities: songs, stories, speaking games.
Introduce written English gradually, linking letters to sounds (phonics).
Avoid tasks where reading the instructions is harder than the language being practised.
Record literacy information in learner profiles (Unit 2).
For adults with limited schooling, use pictures and oral instructions.
Support: oral-only tasks until literacy develops.
Stretch: short reading tasks for confident readers.

blocks.x: A literacy check for young learners:

lines: Show three simple words with pictures (cat, sun, bus). Can the child read them? Show a short sentence in their home language. Can they read it?

blocks.x: Why it matters: a child who cannot yet read a worksheet is being tested on reading, not on the English you meant to practise.

body: Purpose: to show the sequence for emerging readers. Content: three steps: a child listening and singing (‘hear it’); a child speaking with a friend (‘say it’); a child pointing at a word card (‘see it’); a child writing (‘write it’). Style: bright, child-friendly. Board version: not applicable.

items: Read Along by Google (free Android app) for supported reading practice.

blocks.x: Letter cards and picture cards for phonics games.

points.h: One Size Doesn't Fit All Adults Either
pts: Adult learners themselves range widely by educational background and prior language-learning experience.
An adult with strong L1 literacy and prior L2 study benefits from explicit approaches an unschooled adult learner may not.
'Adult learner' is a starting category, not a single teaching template.

items: Ask adults about prior schooling, previous English study, current use of English, and time available.
Group responses: highly educated beginners, experienced users with gaps, learners with limited schooling.
Plan different supports for each group within the same class.
Revisit at mid-course.
Short one-to-one conversations instead of a questionnaire.
Differentiation is the purpose of the activity.

blocks.x: Three adult profiles in one class:

lines: A graduate engineer who reads English well but rarely speaks it.
A shop owner who speaks some English with tourists but cannot write it.
A domestic worker with little schooling who wants to help her children with homework.

blocks.x: Each needs something different, and all three are ‘adult beginners’.

body: Purpose: to show diversity among adults. Content: three portraits side by side, each with a small speech bubble summarizing their need (‘speaking confidence’, ‘writing basics’, ‘reading with my children’). Style: respectful, realistic, inclusive. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Forms (free) for the background questionnaire.

blocks.x: One-to-one conversation at the start of the course.

body: Ask each adult learner one question in the first lesson: ‘What is one thing you want to do in English by the end of this course?’ Write the answers down. At the end of the course, read each learner their answer and ask whether they can now do it.

dek: Unit 16 of 100: the same target language, taught two very differently — cognitive readiness, attention span and motivation all shift the foundations underneath a lesson.

aims.x: This unit compares teaching English to children and to adults. It shows how cognitive development, attention, play, metacognition, motivation, sensitivity to correction and literacy shape what works for each group, and warns against treating either group as uniform.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: adapt grammar teaching to learners’ stage of cognitive development;
plan activity lengths and variety to suit attention spans;
use games, songs and stories as core methodology with young learners;
use metacognitive tasks with adults and older learners;
frame motivation differently for children, teenagers and adults;
calibrate correction to age and social sensitivity;
check literacy assumptions before planning written work;
recognize the diversity within adult groups.

why: Why this matters. Techniques from Units 1–15 aren't age-neutral. Applying an adult-calibrated technique unchanged to a young-learner class — or the reverse — is a common source of failed lessons.

background.x: Age is one of the most visible differences between classes, and one of the most misunderstood. Popular belief says that children learn languages effortlessly and adults struggle. The research picture is more nuanced. Children who begin young in a naturalistic setting, with plenty of exposure, tend to reach higher long-term attainment, particularly in pronunciation. But in classroom settings with limited hours, older learners often make faster progress in the early stages because they can use their knowledge of how language works (Muñoz 2006; Lightbown and Spada 2013). Unit 87 examines the Critical Period Hypothesis in depth.

For the classroom teacher, the more practical point is that children and adults learn differently, not better or worse. Lynne Cameron (2001) emphasizes that children make sense of language through meaningful activity and social interaction: they need language embedded in stories, games and tasks they care about. Annamaria Pinter (2017) adds that young learners’ attention, memory and literacy are still developing, so lessons must be shaped to fit. Adults, by contrast, bring life experience, clear purposes and the ability to reflect on their own learning. Malcolm Knowles’s work on adult learning (1980) stresses that adults learn best when they see the relevance of what they learn to their own goals.

In India, age interacts with language policy. NEP 2020 places strong emphasis on foundational literacy and numeracy in the early grades and recommends learning in the home language during those years, with English introduced as an additional language. The national mission for foundational literacy, NIPUN Bharat, launched in 2021, focuses on ensuring that every child can read with understanding by the end of Grade 3 (Ministry of Education 2021). A teacher of young learners of English therefore works alongside, and builds on, literacy development in other languages.

items: Young learners. Observation checklists for participation in songs, games and retelling; picture-based checks rather than written tests.
Teenagers. Short tasks with private feedback; self-assessment against can-do statements.
Adults. Goal-based assessment: progress towards the goal each learner named.
Literacy tracking. For emerging readers, record words and sentences read each month.
What do you believe about age and language learning? Where does that belief come from?
How long are the activities in your young-learner lessons? How long do children actually attend?
How do you use play in your classes? Is it core or a reward?
How do you find out about adults’ previous schooling and needs?
How does correction affect the teenagers you teach?

perm: Songs used in class must be traditional, original or properly licensed; song lyrics may not be reproduced in the book without permission. Screenshots of Read Along, YouTube Kids, StoryWeaver, Google Forms, Mentimeter or Padlet require permission or replacement with original illustrations.
next: Coming next. Unit 17 turns to another major variable: class size, and how core techniques scale — or fail to scale — into large classes.

terms.def: The theory and practice of teaching adults, which stresses that adults learn best when learning is relevant to their own goals and draws on their experience (Knowles 1980).
The length of time a learner can concentrate on one activity; it is shorter in young children, so lessons for them need frequent changes of activity and pace.
The growth of children’s thinking abilities, such as memory, reasoning and abstraction, over time; it shapes which tasks and explanations suit learners of different ages.

A learner who is just beginning to read, linking sounds to letters and recognizing some familiar words. Teachers plan oral-first activities and introduce written English gradually, building on home-language literacy.
The basic ability to read with understanding and write, expected by the end of Grade 3. NEP 2020 and the NIPUN Bharat mission give it high priority in India’s early grades.
Awareness and control of one’s own thinking and learning, including planning how to approach a task, monitoring understanding and evaluating what worked.
A method of teaching reading by linking letters and letter groups to the sounds they represent, so that learners can decode and blend unfamiliar words.
Learning through purposeful play, such as games, songs, role play and movement, especially with young learners; it is emphasized in NEP 2020 for the foundational stage.

Activities chosen to manage young learners’ energy: stirrers, such as action songs or running dictation, raise energy; settlers, such as colouring or story listening, calm the class. Teachers alternate them across a lesson.
Learners of primary school age, roughly 5 to 12, who learn through activity, play and routine, have short attention spans and need concrete, meaningful tasks.
